It reads `.github/workflows/eval.yml`, which `fast-wall-clock-budget` also parses — that case pins the values the workflow declares, this one pins that those values are what ADR-019 §5's own table derives, so neither subsumes the other. provenance_adr019_s9_2026_08_28: ADR-019 §9 changed what a row in §5's table IS, and this case follows it. The forcing fact is mechanical, not editorial: CI run 33113860608 breached on `invariant` (26.97s, 86/86 passing), and a job that exits at the `invariant` step never runs `fast` — so the row that SETS the ceiling has no `fast` cell. The old two-column shape (one row = one attempt, `invariant` and `fast` side by side, exactly 4 rows) could only hold that observation by dropping it, which censors the sample at precisely the run that moves the number: the disqualifying property IS the breach being measured. So the table is now one row per measured RUN, carrying its id, branch, suite and case count, and the two suites are sampled independently — four slowest runs each. Two clauses got STRONGER rather than weaker in the move: the run id is bound to its measurement by table position instead of being searched for as `eval-gate run <id>` prose anywhere in §5 (the form PR #41 R12 had to bound because it matched an id two paragraphs from the table it sourced), and the citation required in README is now the id of the row carrying each suite's MAXIMUM — the run the ceiling is actually derived from — rather than one id for the whole section. Everything else is unchanged: eight cells cell-by-cell against the workflow comment, README's four `fast` values and both range+ceiling pairs read back FROM the table, one CI band in README, and the workflow's declared ceilings equal to `_band_rule` of each column's max. Still NOT graded, for the reason it never could be from here: that anyone ran these runs (T-R73). Review of PR #72 then falsified the SAMPLE while every published cell transcribed correctly, which is the hole this case still has and now says so: the `fast` column published 112.28s as its fourth row while run 33119673100 had measured 116.01s inside the same window — a fifth-place row under a sentence claiming the four slowest — and the window ended eleven minutes before run 33120495080, the SECOND breaching run (25.61s, 88/88, 65 actions, 8 judge calls). Neither could go red here: this case grades the published cells against two copies and never against the log, so a sample that omits a run is invisible to it (T-R73 is the only route). Both are fixed by stating the window by its ENDPOINTS instead of by a count — every eval-gate run from 33098541355 to 33120495080, 19 runs — and the declared-limitation sentence in the ADR now names the hole. Neither ceiling moved: 26.97 and 117.84 were and are the maxima. Watched red nine ways in the corrected form, each restored to green: (1) ADR `invariant` max 26.97->26.99 — {adr_five_table: [26.99, 25.61, 22.81, 22.71], workflow_comment: [26.97, ...]} plus the README range going stale in the same edit; (2) ADR `fast` max 117.84->117.11, which reds three ways because it also moves WHICH run is the maximum — {readme: does_not_name_the_run_that_sets_the_ceiling, suite: fast, adr_cites: 33113986233}; (3) the second-breach row deleted — {adr_five_table_rows: {fast: 4, invariant: 3}}; (4) the newly added 116.01s `fast` row deleted — {adr_five_table_rows: {fast: 3, invariant: 4}}, the two halves of the review finding each pinned; (5) the ceiling-setting run id altered one digit — {adr_cites: 33113860609}; (6) the WORKFLOW comment edited instead of the ADR, operands swapped; (7) the workflow's declared `invariant` ceiling dropped to 30 — {workflow_declares: 30, adr_five_max: 26.97, rule_gives: 35}, which ALSO fired the site sweep on the amendment's own Ruling line, the demonstration that its live numbers are graded prose and not decoration; (8) README's `fast` list value 116.01->116.09; (9) README's `invariant` range minimum 22.71->22.1, the exact stale value the pre-review table published, so the regression that produced this round is itself pinned.
provenance_pr72_round2_2026_08_28: Round 2 of PR #72 returned eleven findings, none HIGH, and the structural one (R6) is why this key exists. ADR-019's amendment argues its ruling from roughly fifteen CI wall clocks that NOTHING here reads: this check slices section 5's table alone, and the stray-ceiling site sweep matches only integer-and-`s` figures, so a decimal like `26.97s` is invisible to it by construction. The amendment therefore reproduced, in its own body, the defect its ruling exists to correct — CI numbers published without derivation — which is a fourth instance in this PR of a repair creating the class it repairs. The repair chosen was NOT to move those figures into the graded table: section 5 is a record and the amendment is an argument whose force comes from a controlled comparison, and flattening one into the other would destroy it. Instead the ungraded region is DECLARED, ADR-029's 'and nowhere else' clause is struck for naming a one-publisher rule no check enforces, and the amendment carries a count of actual misses rather than a general claim: four figures in that region were wrong in one round and all four were caught by a person reading logs (a case-count span reading 83 to 86 where the table publishes 88; a p90 row computed on the pre-repair 18-run window; a drop-the-breach premise written for one breach after a second entered the sample; and an interval written as twenty minutes that is about 85). None changed a ceiling and none could go red. R9 is the one finding that became MECHANISM rather than disclosure: section 5's claim that its rows run slowest first was unbacked prose, and is now one line — `by[suite] == sorted(by[suite], reverse=True)` — graded on the ADR side only, since the workflow comment is already compared element-wise against the same list. Watched red both ways, each restored: two `invariant` rows swapped gives {suite: invariant, adr_five_table_not_slowest_first: [26.97, 25.61, 22.71, 22.81]}, two `fast` rows swapped the same for that suite, and each also reddens the workflow-comparison clause, which is the belt this line adds braces to. R8 corrected an UNDER-claim rather than an over-claim: the coverage sentence said ten of forty cells were graded, but the eight `suite` cells are load-bearing — the suite cell selects which per-suite list a wall clock joins — so it is eighteen. Demonstrated rather than asserted: flipping one suite cell from `invariant` to `fast` reports {adr_five_table_rows: {fast: 5, invariant: 3}}.
provenance_pr72_round3_2026_08_28: Round 3's serious finding is a grader WEAKENING this PR itself introduced, and it is the reason the row count no longer trusts the suite vocabulary. The reshaped table is parsed per suite by `^\| (\d{6,}) \| [^|]* \| (invariant|fast) \| \d+ \| ([\d.]+)s \|`, which SKIPS any row whose `suite` cell is neither word — where the pre-PR check counted rows and refused a fifth outright. So a bogus row could be published in section 5 with the gate green, and `_in_section_five` exempts that section from the stray-ceiling sweep, so nothing else was looking either. A PR whose entire subject is making CI numbers graded must not leave a hole through which an ungraded one can be published. Fixed by counting id-rows on their SHAPE — `^\| \d{6,} \|[^\n]*\|` — and refusing any count mismatch, so recognition is required rather than assumed. Watched red twice, restored: an injected `| 99999999999 | task/EVIL | banana | 999 | 999.99s |` gives {adr_five_table_unrecognised_rows: 1, id_rows: 9, parsed: 8}, and the same row naming a third real suite (`live`) reports identically — the second is the likelier accident and the one a vocabulary-based count would wave through. R8 was an UNDER-claim confirmed rather than accepted: the eight `suite` cells are load-bearing, so eighteen of forty cells are graded, demonstrated by flipping one cell to get {adr_five_table_rows: {fast: 5, invariant: 3}}. The rest of the round was scope prose, and one of those repairs was itself caught by the GATE rather than by review, which is worth recording because it cuts the other way: the disclosure paragraph wrapped so that `85.` began a line, markdown read it as list item 85, and `published-band-matches-the-ledger` reddened with {adr_six_list_is_not_1_to_n_with_slugs: [..., ['85', '']]}. Section 6's numbered-list rule is graded, so prose that collides with it cannot land — which is precisely the contrast the amendment's own disclosure draws between graded and ungraded regions.
